did_you_know.text: The chapter opens by describing Samaria’s punishment because she rebelled against her God. Alongside the description of destruction, it also warns of harm to children and pregnant women.
The call “Return, Israel” places repentance at the center of the chapter. Sin is portrayed as a failure from which Israel is required to return to the LORD.

Israel is called to bring “words” to the LORD—that is, confession and petition—and to ask, “Forgive all our iniquity and accept what is good.” In this way, prayer and speech are presented as central parts of returning to the LORD.
The phrase “that we may offer the fruit of our lips” presents the lips as bringing the LORD “bulls,” meaning words of thanksgiving and commitment, in language reminiscent of a sacrifice.
The confession includes rejecting three alternative sources of security: Assyria, military strength represented by horses, and idols, which are “the work of our hands.”
The verse concludes by portraying the LORD as one who shows compassion to the fatherless. This image emphasizes his kindness toward those who have no other support.

After the call to repentance, the LORD’s action is described with the words “I will heal their apostasy” and “I will love them freely”—healing and love presented not as something people earn, but as divine grace.
Israel’s renewal is described through images from the natural world: dew, a lily, roots like the cedars of Lebanon, an olive tree, and a vine. These images emphasize both growth and stability.

The blessing described is not merely personal: Israel’s people will once again dwell in the shade, live on grain, and blossom like the vine. In this way, the blessing includes protection, food, and flourishing.

The chapter concludes by saying that Ephraim’s fruit is found in the LORD. It then declares that the LORD’s ways are right: the righteous walk in them, but the rebellious stumble in them. The same path reveals each person’s moral response.
